quote: it doesn’t matter much what their religion says, because whatever they want to do, they can find a religious reason for it
content: The premise rests on an anecdote about the religious people "I meet," and the systematic evidence points the other way. Doctrine visibly changes behavior even when the change is costly. Pregnant Muslim women who fast during Ramadan have children with measurable later deficits in health and schooling (Almond & Mazumder 2011). Longer Ramadan fasting hours lower output growth in Muslim countries while raising reported happiness (Campante & Yanagizawa-Drott 2015). People fast, tithe, refuse transfusions and keep the Sabbath against their immediate desires. Religion is not an endlessly stretchable rationalization, and the essay's analogy for selfishness inherits that false premise.

quote: If you’re genuinely selfish, then why do you want me to be selfish too? Doesn’t that make you concerned for my welfare?
content: The gotcha only works against someone who says "I want what is best for me and nothing else," and the interlocutor never said that. An ethical egoist holds that everyone ought to pursue their own interest. He can consistently advocate that rule for everyone, the way a chess player can want opponents to play by the rules while hoping they lose; Kalin (1975) defends exactly this position. The Randian egoist the dialogue implies goes further and claims that rational interests never conflict, so on his view advocating general egoism is advocating mutual benefit. The essay aims an argument against ethical egoism (a claim about norms) in order to refute psychological egoism (a claim about motives), and neither is quite the view on the table.

quote: And the one said, “You may be right about that last part,” so I marked him down as intelligent.
content: The essay's entire evidence is one unnamed interlocutor's partial concession, and the test for scoring him "intelligent" is that he agreed. The sequences warn elsewhere against exactly this: updating on the pleasure of winning a concession rather than on whether the argument was sound. Nothing in the exchange separates "he saw the point" from "he wanted the conversation to end."

quote: taking into account that scope insensitivity leads many people to be more concerned over one life than the Earth
content: That is not what scope insensitivity is. Scope insensitivity is flat valuation across sizes, such as paying the same for 2,000 birds as for 200,000. Preferring one vivid victim to a large statistical group is the identifiable-victim effect, a different bias with a different mechanism. The footnote's test questions have a problem too. "Would you rather stub your toe or let a stranger be tortured without your knowing" asks for a hypothetical moral choice. FeldmanHall et al. (2012) found that such hypothetical answers differ substantially from what the same people do when real money and real harm are at stake, and the gap runs toward selfishness. The "mischievous questions" measure what people say, which is the last thing an egoist's critic should rely on.
